{{Short description|Icelandic mathematician (1877–1957)}}
'''Ólafur Dan Daníelsson''' (31 October 1877 – 10 December 1957) was an Icelandic mathematician.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Ólafur Daníelsson – Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Danielsson/ |access-date=2023-07-09 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> He was the first Icelandic mathematician to complete a doctoral degree.<ref name=":1" /> He was also the founder of the [[Icelandic Mathematical Society]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Icelandic Mathematical Society |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Societies/Icelandic/ |access-date=2023-07-09 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

== Life ==

=== Early life and education ===
Danielsson was born in [[Viðvík]] in [[Viðvíkursveit]] in [[Skagafjörður|Skagafjördur]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1897, he finished his secondary education in Reykjavík, and in the same year, went to study mathematics in the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Bjarnadóttir |first=Kristín |date=2013 |title=Mathematics Education in Twentieth Century Iceland–Ólafur Daníelsson's Impact. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/284182898 |journal=Dig Where You Stand |volume=3 |pages=65–80}}</ref> [[Hieronymus Georg Zeuthen]] and [[Julius Petersen]] were his university tutors.<ref name=":3" /> In 1900, his first scientific paper was published in the Danish journal ''[[Nyt Tidsskrift for Matematik B]].''<ref name=":3" /> In 1901, he was awarded a gold medal for his mathematical treatise at the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref name=":3" /> In 1904, he was awarded a master's degree, which enabled him to teach in Danish high schools.<ref name=":3" />

Returning to Iceland, he applied to be a mathematics teacher at [[Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík|Reykjavik Junior College]], where he had studied a few years previously.<ref name=":0" /> However, he did not get the job.<ref name=":0" /> The successful applicant was an engineer, Sigurður Thoroddsen.<ref name=":0" />

He started undertaking PhD research.<ref name=":0" /> His thesis built upon the earlier works of [[Hieronymus Georg Zeuthen|Zeuthen]] and other scientists, such as [[Rudolph Clebsch]], [[Guido Castelnuovo|Guido Castelnuevo]] and [[Luigi Cremona]].<ref name=":3" /> In 1909, he submitted his thesis and graduated from the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref name=":0" /> He was the first Icelandic mathematician to be awarded a doctorate.<ref name=":0" />

=== Career ===
He became a private tutor and began writing textbooks.<ref name=":0" /> In 1906, his first textbook, ''Reikningsbók/Arithmetic'', was published.<ref name=":3" /> In 1908, he became the first mathematics teacher in the [[Iceland College of Education|Iceland Teacher College]] when it was first established.<ref name=":3" /> The students were experienced teachers, but had been lacking formal education themselves.<ref name=":3" /> In 1914, his textbook Arithmetic (Reikningsbók) was republished for the students' needs.<ref name=":3" />

In 1919, a mathematics stream at Reykjavík Junior College was founded in response to Danielsson's and his friends' initiative.<ref name=":3" /> He was tasked with its development, with the goal of enabling students to attend the Polytechnic College in [[Copenhagen]] and to pursue university studies in sciences.<ref name=":3" /> Prior to that, students needed to spend a preparatory year abroad.<ref name=":3" />

At the same time, Danielsson started writing high school mathematics textbooks.<ref name=":3" /> In 1920s, his 4 textbooks were republished, including a rewritten version of the Arithmetic book.<ref name=":3" /> Additionally, three new subjects were introduced in Icelandic: ''Um flatarmyndir''/''On plane geometry, Kenslubók í hornafræði/Trigonometry,'' and ''Kenslubók í algebru/A textbook in algebra''.<ref name=":3" /> These three textbooks were groundbreaking, being the first of their kind in Icelandic.<ref name=":3" /> They were adopted for use at [[Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík|Reykjavík High School]], along with the advanced Danish textbooks.<ref name=":3" /> Later, when [[Akureyri High School]] was established in 1930, these textbooks were also incorporated into its curriculum.<ref name=":3" /> The mathematician [[Sigurður Helgason (mathematician)|Sigurdur Helgason]] commented that, "The geometry textbooks by the remarkable mathematician Ólafur Daníelsson, the pioneering founder of mathematics education in Iceland, were written by a man with a real mission".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Helgason |first=Sigurdur |title=The Selected Works of Sigurdur Helgason |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2009 |pages=xiii}}</ref>

In 1941, Daníelsson concluded his teaching career and retired.<ref name=":3" /> His remarkable influence extended over almost seven decades, starting in 1906 when he published his initial textbook and continuing in 1908 when he commenced teaching at Iceland's Teacher College.<ref name=":3" /> His significant impact on mathematics education persisted until 1976 when his textbooks were excluded from the reading list of the national entrance examination.<ref name=":3" /> There is no doubt about his enduring legacy as a devoted mathematician, as his visionary approach helped shape mathematics education in Iceland.<ref name=":3" />

== Research ==
In the 1920s, Daníelsson dedicated himself to advancing the field of algebraic geometry through his research. He actively participated in the [[Scandinavian mathematical congress|Scandinavian Congress of Mathematicians]] held in 1925 and 1927.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Turner |first=Laura E |date=2023 |title=A Richer Gathering: On the History of the Nordic Congress of Mathematicians |url=https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/26750 |journal=European Mathematical Society Magazine |issue=127 |pages=39–44|doi=10.4171/mag/116 |doi-access=free }}</ref> His contributions were instrumental in fostering the development of mathematics in Iceland, which ultimately led to Iceland becoming a full member of the Nordic Congress of Mathematicians in the 1980s.<ref name=":4" />

He published several papers in the Danish ''[[Matematisk Tidsskrift]]'', with notable contributions in the years 1926, 1940, 1945, and 1948.<ref name=":3" /> His research work also appeared in esteemed journals such as [[Mathematische Annalen]], specifically in volumes 102 (1930), 109 (1934), 113 (1937), and 114 (1937).<ref name=":3" />

In 1925, Daníelsson participated in the Sixth [[Scandinavian Congress of Mathematicians]] held in [[Copenhagen]].<ref name=":3" /> Two years later, in 1927, he also attended the seventh congress held in [[Oslo]].<ref name=":3" /> He delivered presentations at both congresses, accompanied by the publication of his papers. His first paper, titled "En Lösning af Malfattis problem" [A solution of Malfatti's Problem], was published in ''[[Matematisk Tidsskrift]]''. Subsequently, he contributed to [[Mathematische Annalen|Matematische Annalen]] with a paper entitled "Überkorrespondierende Punkte der Steinerschen Fläche vierter Ordnung und die Hauptpunkte derselben" (Corresponding Points of Steiner's Surface of Fourth Order and their Principal Points). This journal featured the works of renowned mathematicians such as Einstein, van der Waerden, von Neumann, Landau, Ore, and Kolmogorov, among others, and Daníelsson's paper was among the 44 articles published.<ref name=":3" /> It is worth noting that Danielsson was the ''only'' mathematician from Iceland contributing to [[Scandinavian mathematical journals]] before the second world war.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Siegmund-Schultze |first=Reinhard |date=1850–1950 |title=The Interplay of Various Scandinavian Mathematical Journals (1859–1953) and the Road towards Internationalization |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2018.10.005 |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=354–75 |via=Elsevier Science Direct|hdl=11250/2599889 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Daníelsson's fascination with elementary geometry was evident, as he remarked that "it is difficult to find tasks simpler and more elegant than skillful mathematical problems." His final paper was published in both the [[Journal of the Icelandic Society of Engineers]] in 1946 and [[Matematisk Tidsskrift]] in 1948.<ref name=":3" />

== The Icelandic Mathematical Society ==
On 31 October 1947, the [[Icelandic Mathematical Society]] was founded in [[Reykjavík|Reykjavik]] when Daníelsson was 70. The society records:

“On Friday, 31 October 1947, which was the seventieth birthday of Ólafur Daníelsson, he gathered in his home several men and set up a Society. The purpose of the Society is to promote co-operation and promotion of people in Iceland who have completed a university degree in a mathematical subject. The Society holds meetings at which individual members explain their mathematical topics and, if desired, discussions on the topic will be conducted.”<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Um félagið {{!}} stæ.is |url=http://www.stae.is/isf/isf |access-date=2023-07-09 |website=www.stae.is}}</ref>

The first lecture was delivered by Ólafur Daníelsson himself.<ref name=":0" /> He spoke "about the circle transcribed by the outer circumference of the triangle" and calculated its length relative to the radius of the inscribed circle and the circumference of the triangle. This result has been published in the ''Matematisk Tidsskrift''.<ref name=":0" /> However, this had been a longstanding interest of him, as the initial foundations of this subject could be traced back to an article he wrote in 1900, published in the same journal.<ref name=":0" /> In this regard, the topic itself carried a sense of antiquity, yet it had recently witnessed a fresh comprehension shortly before his presentation.<ref name=":0" />
